name: Umar Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead framer for a family building firm, we put up detached houses on a new estate at the edge of a market town. I've worked for Gerry, the owner, for twenty years, since he had two vans and a cement mixer. My lads and I frame the walls, set the roof trusses and get the roof boarded so the house is dry, then the bricklayers and roofers come in behind us. I'm on site at seven, I've usually got the first wall panel up by half past.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like standing on the top plate when the last truss goes up and you can see the whole street from there. What wears me out is the winter, wet timber and short days. I don't use any of the AI programs, I don't need a computer to tell me how to cut a birdsmouth. Saturdays I coach the under-twelves football, and Sundays it's church with Grace and the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Right, let's start. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, the world still needs people who can build things. At the club I'd say it to the other dads, half of them work in offices and they've been worried. Online, nothing, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, mostly for Josiah. He's fourteen and he wants to come into the trade with me, and I've been telling him a good trade never goes out of fashion. This would prove me right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at all. Keep framing houses for Gerry, keep the savings, which are good, we've been careful. Maybe we'd finally book the trip to see Grace's parents, we've put it off two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The way it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How careful have you been with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've never had a credit card bill we couldn't clear that month. Grace keeps the books at home, she's better at it. We've got about a year put by and a bit in the church credit union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small, anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young lads who don't want to work with their hands. Gerry can't find apprentices, they all want to be on their phones. That's the real problem, not robots.

S0.say: He'd tell the other dads at football that the world still needs people who build things. He doesn't post online.
S0.think: Privately he'd be glad, mostly for his son, who wants to join the trade. It would prove right what he's always told him, that a good trade never goes out of fashion.
S0.do: Keeps framing houses for the same family firm and keeps about a year of savings in place. Finally books the long-postponed trip to see his wife's parents.
S0.feel: Calm, the way he thinks things should be.
S0.quote: He's fourteen and he wants to come into the trade with me, and I've been telling him a good trade never goes out of fashion.
S0.fieldNote: Umar's world is built around loyalty to one employer, family, church and coaching. He doesn't use AI and sees a plateau as confirming his values. His real concern is young people not wanting manual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's always been change, my grandad saw the nail gun come in and he survived. At work I'd say Gerry's not going to replace us with gadgets, he's not that sort. I'd keep my head down and do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I've heard about those factories making whole wall panels with robots. If Gerry buys his walls in, my lads aren't needed for half the job. But Gerry's loyal, and I don't think he'd do that to us quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing much at first. I'd wait and see what Gerry decides, because I trust him. If he wanted me on a course, I'd go, but I wouldn't go looking for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bit of a question mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Gerry did start buying walls from a factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be the one putting them up, I suppose. Somebody still has to stand them straight and nail them off. I'd not like it, mind, I'd miss cutting my own studs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Josiah in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still come in, learn the trade properly. I'd say the same as my dad said to me: turn up, work hard, and there's always a place for you.

S1.say: He'd say there has always been change and his grandfather survived the nail gun. At work he'd insist the owner won't replace the crew with gadgets.
S1.think: Privately he knows factory-made wall panels could halve his crew's work if his employer buys them in. But he trusts his boss's loyalty and doesn't expect it quickly.
S1.do: Changes nothing at first and waits to see what his employer decides. Would attend a course if asked but wouldn't seek one out.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small question mark.
S1.quote: I'd say the same as my dad said to me: turn up, work hard, and there's always a place for you.
S1.fieldNote: His sense of security rests heavily on personal loyalty to his employer. He is aware of factory panels but chooses to trust rather than prepare. The repeated family wisdom about hard work runs deep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built these machines never framed a house in their lives, and they don't care who they put out of work. I'd say it at church, at the club, to anyone. I'd also say we look after our own, we don't wait for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one scares me. If robots can frame a house cheaper, Gerry can't compete unless he buys them, and if he buys them, what's left for me? I've done one thing since I was seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, no trip, no new truck, and put everything into savings and the mortgage. I'd talk to the pastor and the men's group about how we help each other, because there'd be families in trouble. And I'd keep working for Gerry as long as there's anything to do. I wouldn't go chasing some computer course, I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at three in the morning, praying more than I'd admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Josiah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest bit. I'd have to tell him the trade I promised him might not be there. I don't know what I'd tell him to do instead, and that's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. If the government offered support, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if I had to, for the kids. I wouldn't like it. I'd rather the church or my brothers helped, and I'd rather work for it, even if it's sweeping the site.

S2.say: He'd say the people who built the machines never framed a house and don't care who loses work. He'd also say his community looks after its own rather than waiting for handouts.
S2.think: Privately he's scared, because either his employer can't compete or buys robots and doesn't need him. He's done one thing since seventeen.
S2.do: Cuts back hard, cancels the trip and new truck, and puts everything into savings and the mortgage. Organises mutual help through his church's men's group and keeps working for his employer as long as possible without seeking retraining.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at three in the morning and praying more than he'd admit.
S2.quote: I'd have to tell him the trade I promised him might not be there.
S2.fieldNote: This hits his deepest belief, that a trade is a lifelong promise to pass on to his son. He blames tech builders who never did physical work. He'd accept state help only for his children and much prefers church and family support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families and churches and towns to get ready, and we should, instead of waiting for the government. I'd say Gerry and men like him should get first say on how it's used. I'd be quieter than in the fast one, but I'd still say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still frightening, just slower. Five years gets me to forty-eight and Josiah to nineteen, right when he'd finish an apprenticeship. That timing is what bothers me most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the mortgage down hard, so by the time it lands we owe very little. I'd talk to Josiah about doing something alongside his apprenticeship, maybe the electrical side, because they'll need people to fix the machines. And I'd keep working, I'd not change jobs, Gerry's been good to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not up at three every night, but some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it's Josiah. With two years I just protect the family. With five I can maybe steer him somewhere safer before he's in too deep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about yourself with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. Probably I'd keep doing what I do and hope. That's the honest answer, I'm not one for changing.

S3.say: He'd say families, churches and towns have time to prepare and shouldn't wait for government. He'd argue that small builders like his boss should have a say in how the technology is used.
S3.think: Privately it's still frightening, just slower. The timing worries him most, since his son would be finishing an apprenticeship just as it arrives.
S3.do: Pays the mortgage down hard so little is owed by the time AGI lands. Steers his son towards an electrical skill alongside the apprenticeship and stays with his current employer.
S3.feel: Anxious, awake some nights rather than every night.
S3.quote: With five I can maybe steer him somewhere safer before he's in too deep.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time for Umar is time to protect his son's future, not to change himself. He admits plainly he'd keep doing what he does and hope. His faith in community over government stays constant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and the Lord willing, we'll manage. I'd say young people should learn proper skills and look after their families. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is better. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage close to paid, Josiah and Ruth grown. I've got maybe ten good years left on roofs anyway, my back says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep framing for Gerry and keep saving. I'd wait and see what the robots actually look like before doing anything, there's no point jumping at the first one. Josiah could make his own choice by then, with more information.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still coming, but it's further down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd steer Josiah. With ten years, would you still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less. He'd be a grown man by then, twenty-four. I'd give him my view and let him choose, like my dad did with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the day it arrives look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Sunday, church, a roast. Me, fifty-three, with a bad back and a paid-off house. I'd be thankful for what I had, and worried for whoever's starting out.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time and, God willing, they'll manage. He'd urge young people to learn proper skills and look after their families.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels better, reaching fifty-three with the mortgage nearly paid and children grown. His back gives him about ten years on roofs anyway.
S4.do: Keeps framing for the same employer and keeps saving. Waits to see what robots actually look like before acting and leaves his son to make his own choice.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with the threat further down the road.
S4.quote: I've got maybe ten good years left on roofs anyway, my back says so.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade his own body's limits line up with the change, which eases him. He steps back from steering his son, honouring how his own father let him choose. His worry turns outwards to young people starting out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Josiah. What would help is apprenticeships that teach the new skills alongside the old, run by builders like Gerry, not by some office. And help that comes through work, not a cheque in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church, or the club. That's where people would be helped, if it came to it. The government's slow, but the men's group can have a family's fridge full by Tuesday.

headlineQuote: The government's slow, but the men's group can have a family's fridge full by Tuesday.
portrait: Umar Nakamura is a 43-year-old lead framer who has worked twenty years for the same family house builder, married with a son of fourteen and a daughter of eleven. He never uses AI, coaches youth football and leans on church and family far more than on government. He is calm through the plateau and steady change, trusting his boss's loyalty, but alarmed by AGI in two years because it breaks the promise of a trade for his son. More warning doesn't make him change himself; it gives him time to pay down the mortgage and steer his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have to tell his son the trade he promised him might not be there.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships teaching new skills alongside old ones, run by builders rather than offices, and help that comes through work rather than a cheque.
